headline.funnel_interpretation: Egger’s test is generally not recommended when fewer than 10 studies are available.
headline.results_interpretation: The pooled analysis of 2 studies yielded an effect size of 0.68 (95% CI: 0.44–1.07), indicating no statistically significant association between Vitamin C and bladder cancer. Although the point estimate suggests a potential inverse relationship, the confidence interval includes the null. These findings were accompanied by substantial heterogeneity (I² = 53.29%), reflecting considerable variability across studies.

sample_size.excerpt: We investigated the association between plasma carotenoids and vitamin C and risk of urothelial cell carcinoma (UCC) in a case-control study nested within the European Prospective Investigation into Cancer and Nutrition. A total of 856 patients with newly diagnosed UCC were matched with 856 cohort members by sex, age at baseline, study center, date and time of blood collection, and fasting status.

studies.Study: Bruemmer B et al. (1996) [PMID: 8781464] — estimate 1 · Mixed
studies.Reference: Nutrient intake in relation to bladder cancer among middle-aged men and women.
studies.Title: Nutrient intake in relation to bladder cancer among middle-aged men and women.
studies.Authors: Bruemmer B, White E, Vaughan TL, Cheney CL
studies.Population: Caucasian men and women aged 45-65 years in King, Pierce, or Snohomish counties, western Washington
studies.comparison_type: Highest versus lowest quartile of dietary vitamin C intake, adjusted for calories

sample_size.excerpt: Bladder cancer cases (n = 262) were identified from the Surveillance, Epidemiology, and End Results Program cancer registry for western Washington, and controls (n = 405) were identified through random digit dialing. Cases were diagnosed between January 1987 and June 1990, and eligible subjects were Caucasian, aged 45-65 years, and residents of King, Pierce, or Snohomish counties.
sample_size.location: abstract, methods; total_n derived from reported group counts 262 + 405 = 667

cases.excerpt: Bladder cancer cases (n = 262) were identified from the Surveillance, Epidemiology, and End Results Program cancer registry for western Washington, and controls (n = 405) were identified through random digit dialing. Cases were diagnosed between January 1987 and June 1990, and eligible subjects were Caucasian, aged 45-65 years, and residents of King, Pierce, or Snohomish counties.

effect_size.excerpt: An inverse association was found between the risk of bladder cancer and dietary retinol (odds ratio (OR) across quartiles: 1.00, 1.09, 0.97, and 0.52; 95% CI 0.29-0.97; trend p value = 0.03) and dietary vitamin C (OR across quartiles: 1.00, 0.96, 0.67, and 0.50; 95% CI 0.28-0.88; trend p value = 0.009), adjusted for calories.

confidence_interval.excerpt: An inverse association was found between the risk of bladder cancer and dietary retinol (odds ratio (OR) across quartiles: 1.00, 1.09, 0.97, and 0.52; 95% CI 0.29-0.97; trend p value = 0.03) and dietary vitamin C (OR across quartiles: 1.00, 0.96, 0.67, and 0.50; 95% CI 0.28-0.88; trend p value = 0.009), adjusted for calories.

comparison.excerpt: Odds ratios and their 95% confidence intervals for highest versus lowest level of intake were examined.

design.excerpt: This population-based case-control study examined the association between selected nutrients, foods, and diet behaviors and bladder cancer.

timing.excerpt: Cases were diagnosed between January 1987 and June 1990

continent.excerpt: residents of King, Pierce, or Snohomish counties

ethnicity.excerpt: eligible subjects were Caucasian, aged 45-65 years

exposure_measurement.excerpt: Subjects completed a self-administered, 71-item food frequency questionnaire

gender.excerpt: Nutrient intake in relation to bladder cancer among middle-aged men and women.

smoking_status.excerpt: included adjustment for age, sex, smoking (current, former, never), and county
